title: Book 2, Chapter 6 — Beginning of the Peloponnesian War—First Invasion of Attica—Funeral Oration of Pericles
paragraphs: The war between the Athenians and the Peloponnesians and the allies on either side now really begins. From this point on, all communication except through heralds ceased, and hostilities were begun and prosecuted without a break. The history follows the chronological order of events, by summers and winters.

The thirty years’ truce that was made after the conquest of Euboea lasted fourteen years. In the fifteenth, in the forty-eighth year of the priestess-ship of Chrysis at Argos, in the ephorate of Aenesias at Sparta, in the last month but two of the archonship of Pythodorus at Athens, and six months after the battle of Potidæa, just at the beginning of spring, a Theban force a little over three hundred strong, under the command of their Boeotarchs, Pythangelus, son of Phyleides, and Diemporus, son of Onetorides, made an armed entry into Plataea — a town in Boeotia allied with Athens — about the first watch of the night. The gates were opened to them by a Plataean named Naucleides, who, with his party, had invited them in. They intended to put to death the citizens of the opposite faction, hand the city over to Thebes, and so secure power for themselves. The arrangements had been made through Eurymachus, son of Leontiades, a man of great influence at Thebes. For Plataea had always been at odds with Thebes; and Thebes, foreseeing that war was at hand, wanted to surprise her old enemy in peacetime, before hostilities had actually broken out. This was how they got in so easily, unobserved: no guard had been posted. Once the soldiers had grounded arms in the marketplace, those who had let them in wanted them to set to work at once and go to the houses of their enemies. The Thebans refused, and decided instead to make a conciliatory proclamation and, if possible, to come to a friendly understanding with the citizens. Their herald accordingly invited any who wished to take their old place in the confederacy of their countrymen to ground arms with them; they thought the city would readily come over to them this way.

When the Plataeans realized that the Thebans were inside their gates and that the town had been suddenly seized, they panicked and assumed that more had entered than was in fact the case — the night kept them from seeing clearly. So they came to terms, accepted the proposal, and made no move; especially since the Thebans offered no violence to anyone. But somehow, during the negotiations, they found out how few the Thebans really were and decided they could easily attack and overpower them, since the great mass of Plataeans was opposed to revolting from Athens. They made up their minds to try it. By digging through the party walls of their houses, they were able to join one another without being seen going through the streets. Across the streets they placed wagons without the animals, to serve as barricades, and arranged everything else as the moment required. When everything had been done that circumstances allowed, they waited their chance and went out of their houses against the enemy. It was still night, though daybreak was near: in daylight they thought their attack would meet men full of courage and on equal terms with their assailants, while in the dark it would fall on troops in a panic, who would also be at a disadvantage from the locals’ knowledge of the ground. So they made their assault at once and closed with the enemy as fast as they could.

The Thebans, realizing they had been outwitted, immediately closed up and tried to repel the attacks made on them. Two or three times they beat their assailants back. But the men shouted and charged at them, the women and slaves screamed and yelled from the houses and pelted them with stones and tiles, and on top of all this it had been raining hard all night; so in the end their courage gave way and they turned and fled through the town. Most of the fugitives had no idea of the right ways out, and this — together with the mud, the darkness from a moon in its last quarter, and the fact that their pursuers knew the ground and could easily cut off their escape — proved fatal to many. The only gate open was the one they had come in by, and a Plataean shut even that, driving the spike of a javelin into the bar instead of the bolt; so even there the way out was gone. They were now hunted all over the town. Some climbed the wall and threw themselves over, in most cases fatally. One group managed to find a deserted gate and, getting an axe from a woman, cut through the bar; but they were soon spotted, and only a few got out. Others were cut off in small groups in different parts of the city. The largest and most compact body burst into a big building next to the city wall: the doors on the street side happened to be open, and the Thebans imagined these were the gates of the town and that there was a passage straight through to the outside. The Plataeans, seeing their enemies trapped, debated whether to set fire to the building and burn them where they stood, or whether to do something else with them. In the end the men inside, along with the rest of the Theban survivors found wandering about the town, surrendered themselves and their arms unconditionally to the Plataeans.

While this was happening to the men inside Plataea, the rest of the Thebans, who were supposed to have joined them in full force before daybreak in case anything went wrong with the party that had entered, got the news of the affair on the road and pressed on to help. Now Plataea is nearly eight miles from Thebes, and their march was slowed by the rain that had fallen in the night, since the river Asopus had risen and was hard to cross. So, having to march in the rain and being held up at the river, they arrived too late and found their whole party either killed or captured. When they learned what had happened, they at once formed a plan against the Plataeans outside the city. The attack had come in peacetime and was completely unexpected, so naturally there were people and livestock out in the fields; the Thebans wanted, if possible, to take some prisoners they could exchange for their own men in the town, in case any had been taken alive. That was their plan. But the Plataeans suspected what they were up to almost before it was formed. Worried about their fellow citizens outside the town, they sent a herald to the Thebans, reproaching them for their unscrupulous attempt to seize the city in peacetime, and warning them not to harm anyone outside it. If the warning was ignored, they threatened to put to death the men they were holding; but they added that, if the Thebans withdrew from their territory, they would hand the prisoners over to their friends. That is the Theban version of events, and they say an oath was given them. The Plataeans, on the other hand, do not admit any promise of an immediate handover, but make it conditional on later negotiation; and they deny the oath altogether. Whatever the truth, when the Thebans withdrew from their territory without doing any harm, the Plataeans hastily brought in whatever they had in the country and at once put the prisoners to death. The prisoners numbered one hundred and eighty; Eurymachus, the man with whom the traitors had negotiated, was one of them.

After this the Plataeans sent a messenger to Athens, gave the dead back to the Thebans under truce, and arranged things in the city as best suited the present emergency. The Athenians meanwhile, having had word of the affair sent to them as soon as it happened, had immediately seized all the Boeotians in Attica and sent a herald to the Plataeans forbidding them to take final action against their Theban prisoners without instructions from Athens. The news of the men’s deaths had not yet arrived; the first messenger had left Plataea just as the Thebans were entering it, the second just after their defeat and capture, so there was no later news. The Athenians thus sent their orders without knowing the facts; and the herald, on arrival, found the men already dead. After this the Athenians marched to Plataea and brought in supplies, left a garrison there, and took away the women and children, as well as those of the men who were least able to fight.

After the affair at Plataea, the treaty had been broken by an open act, and Athens at once prepared for war, as did Lacedaemon and her allies. They resolved to send embassies to the King and to such other barbarian powers as either side could look to for help, and they tried to ally themselves with the independent states at home. Lacedaemon, in addition to her existing fleet, ordered the states that had declared for her in Italy and Sicily to build ships up to a grand total of five hundred — each city’s quota fixed by its size — and to provide a specified sum of money. Until these were ready, they were to remain neutral and to admit single Athenian ships into their harbours. Athens, on her part, reviewed her existing confederacy and sent embassies to the places more immediately around the Peloponnese — Corcyra, Cephallenia, Acarnania, and Zacynthus — realizing that, if these could be relied on, she could carry the war right around the Peloponnese.

And it was only natural that both sides should nurse the boldest hopes and put forth their utmost strength. Zeal is always at its peak at the start of an undertaking; and on this particular occasion the Peloponnese and Athens were both full of young men whose inexperience made them eager to take up arms, while the rest of Hellas stood watching with strained excitement at the clash of its leading cities. Predictions were being recited everywhere, and oracles chanted by the people who collect them — and not just in the contending cities. Some time before this, too, there had been an earthquake at Delos, the first in the memory of the Hellenes. This was said and thought to foreshadow the events ahead; indeed, nothing of the kind that happened was allowed to pass without comment. Public sympathy ran strongly with the Lacedaemonians, especially as they proclaimed themselves the liberators of Hellas. No private or public effort that could help them by word or deed was left undone; everyone felt the cause suffered wherever he himself could not see to it. So general was the indignation against Athens, whether by those who wanted to escape from her empire or those afraid of being absorbed by it. Such were the preparations and such the feelings with which the contest opened.

The allies of the two belligerents were these. On the Lacedaemonian side: all the Peloponnesians within the Isthmus except the Argives and Achaeans, who were neutral; Pellene was the only Achaean city that joined in the war from the start, though the others followed her lead later. Outside the Peloponnese: the Megarians, Locrians, Boeotians, Phocians, Ambraciots, Leucadians, and Anactorians. Of these, ships were supplied by the Corinthians, Megarians, Sicyonians, Pellenians, Eleans, Ambraciots, and Leucadians; cavalry by the Boeotians, Phocians, and Locrians. The other states sent infantry. That was the Lacedaemonian confederacy. The Athenian confederacy consisted of the Chians, Lesbians, Plataeans, the Messenians at Naupactus, most of the Acarnanians, the Corcyraeans, the Zacynthians, and various tributary cities in the following regions: Caria on the coast with her Dorian neighbours, Ionia, the Hellespont, the Thracian towns, the islands lying between the Peloponnese and Crete to the east, and all the Cyclades except Melos and Thera. Of these, ships were supplied by Chios, Lesbos, and Corcyra; the rest provided infantry and money. Such were the allies of either side, and such their resources for the war.

Right after the affair at Plataea, Lacedaemon sent orders round to the cities in the Peloponnese and the rest of her confederacy to prepare troops and the supplies needed for a campaign abroad, with the aim of invading Attica. Each state was ready at the appointed time, and they assembled at the Isthmus, each city contributing two-thirds of its total force. When the whole army had mustered, the Lacedaemonian king, Archidamus, the leader of the expedition, called together the generals of all the states and the principal officers, and addressed them as follows:

“Peloponnesians and allies, our fathers fought many campaigns both within and outside the Peloponnese, and the older men among us here are not without experience of war. Yet we have never set out with a larger force than this, and remarkable as our numbers and quality are, so too is the power of the state we are marching against. We must not, then, show ourselves inferior to our ancestors, or unequal to our own reputation. The hopes and attention of all Hellas are fixed on this effort, and her sympathy is with the enemy of hated Athens. Therefore, however large the invading army may seem, however certain it may appear to some that our adversary will not meet us in the field, this is no excuse for the slightest carelessness on the march. The officers and men of each city must always be ready for danger to fall on their own quarter. The course of war cannot be foreseen, and its attacks are usually dictated by the impulse of the moment; and where overconfidence has scorned preparation, a wise wariness has often been able to hold its own against superior numbers. Confidence is not out of place in an army of invasion, but in enemy country it should also be matched by the precaution of caution: troops on this footing are best inspired to strike a blow and best protected against receiving one. In this case, the city we are marching against, far from being defenceless, is excellently equipped at every point. So we have every reason to expect that the Athenians will take the field against us; and that, if they have not set out before we are there, they certainly will when they see us in their territory wasting and destroying their property. Men are always exasperated at suffering injuries they are not used to and at seeing them inflicted before their eyes; and where they are least inclined to think things through, they rush most furiously into action. The Athenians are the people most likely to do this, since they aim to rule the rest of the world, and are more in the habit of invading and ravaging their neighbours’ territory than of seeing their own treated the same way. Considering, then, the power of the state we are marching against, and the size of the reputation we will win or lose for our ancestors and ourselves depending on how it ends, follow where you may be led, and remember to treat discipline and vigilance as of first importance, and to obey the orders sent to you promptly. Nothing contributes so much to the credit and safety of an army as the union of large bodies under a single discipline.”

With this brief speech, Archidamus dismissed the assembly. He then sent off Melesippus, son of Diacritus, a Spartan, to Athens, in case she might be more inclined to submit on seeing the Peloponnesians actually on the march. But the Athenians did not admit him into the city or to their assembly; Pericles had already carried a motion against admitting any herald or embassy from the Lacedaemonians once they had marched out.

The herald was therefore sent away without an audience, and ordered to be beyond the frontier that same day; in future, if those who had sent him had any proposition to make, they were to withdraw to their own territory before dispatching embassies to Athens. An escort was sent with Melesippus to keep him from communicating with anyone. When he reached the frontier and was about to be dismissed, he left with these words: “This day will be the beginning of great misfortunes for the Hellenes.” As soon as he reached camp and Archidamus learned that the Athenians still had no thought of submitting, he at last began his march and advanced with his army into their territory. Meanwhile the Boeotians, having sent their contingent and cavalry to join the Peloponnesian expedition, marched on Plataea with the rest and laid waste the country.

While the Peloponnesians were still gathering at the Isthmus, or marching before they invaded Attica, Pericles, son of Xanthippus, one of the ten Athenian generals, realized the invasion was about to happen. It occurred to him that Archidamus, who happened to be his personal friend, might possibly bypass his estate without ravaging it. He might do this either as a personal favour or under instructions from Lacedaemon, with the aim of stirring up suspicion against him — much as had been tried before with the demand for the expulsion of the accursed family. Pericles therefore took the precaution of announcing in the Athenian assembly that, although Archidamus was his friend, this friendship would not be allowed to harm the state; and that if the enemy made an exception of his houses and lands and did not pillage them, he was at once handing them over as public property, so that no suspicion would attach to him. He also gave the citizens advice on their present situation in the same vein as before. They were to prepare for the war and to bring in their property from the country. They were not to go out to battle, but to come into the city and guard it, and to have ready their fleet, in which their real strength lay. They were also to keep a tight rein on their allies, since the strength of Athens was drawn from the money those payments brought in; and success in war depends mainly on conduct and capital — there was no reason for despondency. Apart from other sources of revenue, an average income of six hundred talents of silver came in from the tribute of the allies. There were still six thousand talents of coined silver in the Acropolis, out of nine thousand seven hundred that had once been there, from which money had been taken for the porch of the Acropolis, the other public buildings, and Potidæa. This did not include the uncoined gold and silver in public and private offerings, the sacred vessels for the processions and games, the Median spoils, and similar resources, amounting to five hundred talents. To this he added the treasures of the other temples. These were not insignificant and could fairly be used. If they were ever absolutely driven to it, they could even take the gold ornaments off Athene’s own statue; for the figure contained forty talents of pure gold, and it was all removable. This could be used for survival, but every penny had to be paid back. Such was the financial position — and a satisfactory one. Then they had an army of thirteen thousand heavy infantry, plus another sixteen thousand in the garrisons and on home duty at Athens. That was the number on guard at first, in the event of an invasion: it consisted of the oldest and youngest levies and the resident aliens with heavy armour. The Phaleric wall ran for four miles before joining the wall around the city; of this last, nearly five miles were guarded, though part was left without a guard — the stretch between the Long Wall and the Phaleric. Then there were the Long Walls to Piraeus, a distance of about four and a half miles, the outer of which was manned. Lastly, the circuit of Piraeus together with Munychia was nearly seven and a half miles; only half of this, however, was guarded. Pericles also pointed out that they had twelve hundred horse, including mounted archers, sixteen hundred foot archers, and three hundred galleys fit for service. Such were the resources of Athens in each department when the Peloponnesian invasion was looming and hostilities were beginning. Pericles also urged his usual arguments for expecting a favourable outcome to the war.

The Athenians took his advice and began bringing in their wives and children from the country, along with all their household furniture, even the woodwork of their houses, which they took down. Their sheep and cattle they sent across to Euboea and the islands nearby. But they found the move hard, since most of them had always been used to living in the country.

From very early times this had been more the case with the Athenians than with others. Under Cecrops and the first kings, down to the reign of Theseus, Attica had always consisted of a number of independent townships, each with its own town hall and magistrates. Except in times of danger the king at Athens was not consulted; in normal seasons they ran their government and settled their affairs without his involvement; sometimes they even went to war against him, as in the case of the Eleusinians under Eumolpus against Erechtheus. With Theseus, however, they had a king of equal intelligence and power. One of the chief features of his reorganization of the country was to abolish the council-chambers and magistrates of the smaller cities and merge them into the single council-chamber and town hall of the present capital. Individuals could still enjoy their private property as before, but they were now compelled to have only one political centre — Athens — which thus counted all the inhabitants of Attica among her citizens. So when Theseus died he left a great state behind him. From him, indeed, dates the Synoecia, or Feast of Union, which is paid for by the state and which the Athenians still hold in honour of the goddess. Before this, the city consisted of the present citadel and the district just below it, facing more towards the south. This is shown by the fact that the temples of the other deities, besides that of Athene, are in the citadel; and even those that are outside it are mostly in this part of the city — like the temple of Olympian Zeus, of Pythian Apollo, of Earth, and of Dionysus in the Marshes (the same in whose honour the older Dionysia are still celebrated to this day in the month of Anthesterion, not only by the Athenians but by their Ionian descendants too). There are other ancient temples in this quarter as well. The fountain too, which since the alteration made by the tyrants has been called Enneacrounos, or Nine Pipes, but which when the spring was open went by the name of Callirhoe, or Fairwater, was in those days, because it was so close, used for the most important purposes. Indeed, the old custom of using its water before marriage and for other sacred purposes is still kept up. And from their old residence in that quarter, the citadel is still called by the Athenians “the city.”

So the Athenians long lived scattered across Attica in independent townships. Even after the centralization of Theseus, old habit still prevailed; from early times down to the present war, most Athenians still lived in the country with their families and households, and were therefore not at all inclined to move now, especially as they had only just restored their establishments after the Median invasion. Their distress and resentment ran deep at having to abandon their houses and the hereditary temples of the ancient way of life, and at having to change their habits and say goodbye to what each regarded as his native city.

When they reached Athens, only a few had houses of their own to go to or could find shelter with friends or relatives; by far the greater number had to take up quarters in the parts of the city not built over and in the temples and chapels of the heroes — except the Acropolis, the temple of the Eleusinian Demeter, and the other places that were always kept closed. The plot of ground below the citadel called the Pelasgian had been forbidden to occupation by a curse, and there was also an ominous fragment of a Pythian oracle which said:
Leave the Pelasgian parcel desolate, Woe worth the day that men inhabit it!

Yet this too was now built over in the necessity of the moment. In my opinion, if the oracle came true, it did so in the opposite sense to what was expected. The misfortunes of the state did not come from the unlawful occupation; rather, the necessity of the occupation came from the war. Though the god did not say so, he foresaw that it would be an evil day for Athens when the plot came to be inhabited. Many people also took up quarters in the towers of the walls or wherever else they could. When everyone had come in, the city was too small to hold them; though afterwards they divided the Long Walls and a large part of Piraeus into lots and settled there. All this while great attention was being given to the war: the allies were being mustered and a force of a hundred ships was being equipped for the Peloponnese. Such was the state of preparation at Athens.

Meanwhile the Peloponnesian army was advancing. The first town they came to in Attica was Oenoe, where they intended to enter the country. Sitting down before it, they prepared to assault the wall with engines and other means. Oenoe, on the border between Athens and Boeotia, was of course a walled town and was used as a fortress by the Athenians in time of war. So the Peloponnesians prepared their assault, and wasted some valuable time in front of the place. This delay brought heavy criticism on Archidamus. Even during the build-up to the war he had been thought weak and pro-Athenian for the half-measures he had advocated; and after the army had assembled, he had further damaged his reputation by his loitering at the Isthmus and the slowness of the rest of the march. But all of that was nothing compared with the delay at Oenoe. During this interval the Athenians were bringing in their property; and the Peloponnesians believed that a quick advance would have caught everything still out, if it had not been for his procrastination. That was the army’s mood toward Archidamus during the siege. He himself, it is said, expected that the Athenians would shrink from letting their land be wasted and would submit while it was still untouched; that is why he held back.

But after he had assaulted Oenoe and every attempt to take it had failed, and no herald came from Athens, he at last broke up his camp and invaded Attica. This was about eighty days after the Theban attempt on Plataea, in the middle of summer when the corn was ripe. Archidamus, son of Zeuxis, king of Lacedaemon, was in command. Encamping at Eleusis and on the Thriasian plain, they began their ravages, and after putting some Athenian horse to flight at a place called Rheiti, or the Brooks, they advanced, keeping Mount Aegaleus on their right, through Cropia, until they reached Acharnae, the largest of the Athenian demes or townships. Sitting down before it, they made camp there and continued their ravages for a long time.

The reason Archidamus stayed in battle order at Acharnae during this incursion, instead of going down into the plain, is said to have been this. He hoped the Athenians might be tempted, by the size of their younger generation and the unprecedented strength of their armed services, to come out to battle and try to stop the destruction of their lands. Accordingly, since they had not met him at Eleusis or on the Thriasian plain, he tested whether they could be provoked to a sortie by the spectacle of a camp at Acharnae. He thought the place itself was a good site for a camp; and he reckoned that such an important segment of the state as the three thousand heavy infantry of the Acharnians would refuse to put up with the ruin of their property and would force a battle on the rest of the citizens. On the other hand, if the Athenians did not take the field during this incursion, he could safely ravage the plain in future invasions and push his advance right up to the walls of Athens. After the Acharnians had lost their own property, they would be less willing to risk themselves for that of their neighbours; and so there would be division in the Athenian counsels. Those were Archidamus’ motives for staying at Acharnae.

In the meantime, as long as the army was at Eleusis and on the Thriasian plain, hopes were still held that it would not advance any closer. It was remembered that Pleistoanax, son of Pausanias, king of Lacedaemon, had invaded Attica with a Peloponnesian army fourteen years before but had retreated without going further than Eleusis and Thria — which had in fact been the reason for his exile from Sparta, since it was thought he had been bribed to retreat. But when the Athenians saw the army at Acharnae, barely seven miles from Athens, they lost all patience. Their territory was being ravaged before their very eyes — a sight the young men had never seen before, and the old only in the Median wars — and they naturally took it as a grievous insult. The determination was universal, especially among the young men, to march out and stop it. Knots formed in the streets and broke into hot debate; for some warmly recommended the proposed sortie, others opposed it. Oracles of every kind were recited by the collectors and found eager hearers among one side or the other. The Acharnians were the loudest in pressing for the sortie, since they made up no small part of the state’s army and it was their land that was being ravaged. In short, the whole city was in a state of high agitation. Pericles was the target of general indignation; his earlier counsels were completely forgotten; he was abused for not leading out the army he commanded, and was held responsible for the whole of the public suffering.

He, meanwhile, seeing anger and folly in the ascendant for the moment, and confident in the wisdom of his refusal to fight, would not call either an assembly or a meeting of the people, fearing the disastrous results of a debate driven by passion rather than prudence. He devoted himself to the defence of the city and kept it as quiet as possible, while constantly sending out cavalry to prevent raids on the lands near the city by stray parties of the enemy. There was a minor affair at Phrygia between a squadron of Athenian horse with the Thessalians and the Boeotian cavalry, in which the Athenians had rather the better of it until the heavy infantry came up to support the Boeotians, when the Thessalians and Athenians were routed and lost a few men, whose bodies, however, were recovered the same day without a truce. The next day the Peloponnesians set up a trophy. An ancient alliance brought the Thessalians to Athens’ aid; the contingents that came were from Larisa, Pharsalus, Cranon, Pyrasus, Gyrton, and Pherae. The Larisaean commanders were Polymedes and Aristonus, two party leaders in Larisa; the Pharsalian general was Menon; each of the other cities had its own commander as well.

In the meantime the Peloponnesians, since the Athenians did not come out to engage them, broke camp from Acharnae and ravaged some of the demes between Mount Parnes and Brilessus. While they were in Attica, the Athenians sent off the hundred ships they had been preparing against the Peloponnese, with a thousand heavy infantry and four hundred archers on board, under the command of Carcinus, son of Xenotimus, Proteas, son of Epicles, and Socrates, son of Antigenes. This force weighed anchor and started its cruise. The Peloponnesians, after staying in Attica as long as their provisions held out, retired through Boeotia by a different route from the one by which they had come in. As they passed Oropus, they ravaged the territory of Graea, which the Oropians hold from Athens, and on reaching the Peloponnese they broke up to their respective cities.

After they had retired, the Athenians set up guards by land and sea at the points at which they meant to keep regular stations during the war. They also resolved to set apart a special fund of a thousand talents from the money on the Acropolis. This was not to be spent; the current expenses of the war were to be covered some other way. If anyone moved or put to the vote a proposal to use the money for any purpose except defending the city in the event of an enemy fleet attacking by sea, it was to be a capital offence. Along with this sum they also set aside a special fleet of one hundred galleys — the best ships of each year, with their captains. None of these were to be used except with the money, and only against the same kind of peril, should it arise.

Meanwhile the Athenians in the hundred ships round the Peloponnese, reinforced by a Corcyraean squadron of fifty ships and others from the allies in those parts, cruised the coasts and ravaged the country. Among other places, they landed in Laconia and made an assault on Methone, where there was no garrison and the wall was weak. As it happened, Brasidas, son of Tellis, a Spartan, was in command of a guard for the defence of the district. On hearing of the attack, he hurried with a hundred heavy infantry to relieve the besieged, and dashing through the Athenian army, which was scattered over the country with its attention on the wall, he threw himself into Methone. He lost a few men in forcing his way in, but he saved the place and won the gratitude of Sparta by his exploit, becoming the first officer to gain such recognition in the war. The Athenians at once weighed anchor and continued their cruise. Touching at Pheia in Elis, they ravaged the country for two days and defeated a picked force of three hundred men who had come from the vale of Elis and the immediate neighbourhood to the rescue. But a stiff squall came down on them, and not wanting to face it in a place with no harbour, most of them went on board their ships, doubled Point Ichthys, and sailed into the port of Pheia. In the meantime the Messenians, and some others who could not get on board, marched over by land and took Pheia. The fleet later sailed round, picked them up, and put to sea; Pheia was abandoned, since the main army of the Eleans had now come up. The Athenians continued their cruise and ravaged other places along the coast.

About the same time the Athenians sent thirty ships to cruise around Locris and to guard Euboea as well; Cleopompus, son of Clinias, was in command. Making landings from the fleet, he ravaged certain places along the coast, captured Thronium and took hostages from it, and defeated at Alope the Locrians who had assembled to resist him.

During the summer the Athenians also expelled the Aeginetans, with their wives and children, from Aegina, on the grounds that they had been the chief agents in bringing the war on them. Besides, Aegina lay so close to the Peloponnese that it seemed safer to send their own colonists to hold it; the settlers were sent out shortly afterwards. The exiled Aeginetans found refuge in Thyrea, which Lacedaemon gave them — not only because of her quarrel with Athens, but also because the Aeginetans had put her under obligation at the time of the earthquake and the Helot revolt. The territory of Thyrea is on the frontier between Argolis and Laconia, reaching down to the sea. Those Aeginetans who did not settle here were scattered over the rest of Hellas.

The same summer, at the beginning of a new lunar month — the only time, by the way, at which it appears possible — the sun was eclipsed after noon. After it had taken the form of a crescent and some of the stars had come out, it returned to its natural shape.

During the same summer Nymphodorus, son of Pythes, an Abderite whose sister was married to Sitalces, was made the Athenians’ proxenus and summoned to Athens. They had hitherto considered him their enemy; but he had great influence with Sitalces, and they wanted this prince as their ally. Sitalces was the son of Teres and king of the Thracians. Teres, the father of Sitalces, had been the first to establish the great Odrysian kingdom on a scale quite unknown to the rest of Thrace, since a large part of the Thracians were independent. This Teres is in no way related to the Tereus who married Pandion’s daughter Procne from Athens; indeed they did not even belong to the same part of Thrace. Tereus lived in Daulis, in what is now called Phocis, but which at that time was inhabited by Thracians. It was in this land that the women perpetrated the outrage on Itys, and many of the poets, when they mention the nightingale, call it the Daulian bird. Besides, Pandion in arranging an alliance for his daughter would consider the advantages of mutual help, and would naturally prefer a match at this moderate distance to the journey of many days that separates Athens from the Odrysians. Again the names are different; and this Teres was king of the Odrysians — the first, by the way, to attain any power. Sitalces, his son, was now sought as an ally by the Athenians, who wanted his help in the reduction of the Thracian towns and of Perdiccas. Coming to Athens, Nymphodorus concluded the alliance with Sitalces, made his son Sadocus an Athenian citizen, and promised to bring the Thracian war to a close by persuading Sitalces to send the Athenians a force of Thracian horse and targeteers. He also reconciled the Athenians with Perdiccas, and got them to restore Therme to him, on which Perdiccas at once joined the Athenians and Phormio in an expedition against the Chalcidians. So Sitalces, son of Teres, king of the Thracians, and Perdiccas, son of Alexander, king of the Macedonians, became allies of Athens.

Meanwhile the Athenians in the hundred ships were still cruising round the Peloponnese. After taking Sollium, a town belonging to Corinth, and presenting the city and its territory to the Acarnanians of Palaira, they stormed Astacus, expelled its tyrant Evarchus, and brought the place into their confederacy. Next they sailed to the island of Cephallenia and brought it over without using force. Cephallenia lies off Acarnania and Leucas and consists of four states — Pale, Crane, Same, and Pronae. Not long afterwards the fleet returned to Athens. Towards the autumn of this year the Athenians invaded the Megarid with their full levy, including the resident aliens, under the command of Pericles, son of Xanthippus. The Athenians in the hundred ships round the Peloponnese, on their way home, had just reached Aegina when, hearing that the citizens at home were in full force at Megara, they sailed over and joined them. This was without doubt the largest army of Athenians ever assembled, the state being still in the flower of her strength and not yet visited by the plague. A full ten thousand heavy infantry were in the field, all Athenian citizens, besides the three thousand before Potidæa. The resident aliens who joined the incursion were at least three thousand strong, and there was a great mass of light troops besides. They ravaged most of the territory and then withdrew. Other incursions into the Megarid were made by the Athenians annually during the war, sometimes with cavalry alone, sometimes with all their forces. This continued until the capture of Nisaea. Atalanta also, the desert island off the Opuntian coast, was towards the end of this summer turned into a fortified post by the Athenians, to keep privateers from sailing out of Opus and the rest of Locris and plundering Euboea. Such were the events of this summer after the return of the Peloponnesians from Attica.

In the following winter the Acarnanian Evarchus, wanting to return to Astacus, persuaded the Corinthians to sail over with forty ships and fifteen hundred heavy infantry and reinstate him; he himself also hired some mercenaries. In command of the force were Euphamidas, son of Aristonymus, Timoxenus, son of Timocrates, and Eumachus, son of Chrysis. They sailed over and reinstated him; and after failing in an attempt on some places along the Acarnanian coast that they wanted to gain, they began their voyage home. Coasting along, they touched at Cephallenia and made a descent on Cranian territory. Losing some men through the treachery of the Cranians, who fell on them suddenly after agreeing to terms, they put to sea in some haste and went home.

In the same winter the Athenians gave a public funeral to those who had been the first to fall in this war. It was a custom of their ancestors, and the manner is as follows. Three days before the ceremony the bones of the dead are laid out in a tent that has been set up; and friends bring to their relatives whatever offerings they wish. In the funeral procession, cypress coffins are carried in carts, one for each tribe, with the bones of the deceased placed in the coffin of their own tribe. Among them is carried one empty bier, decked out for the missing — that is, for those whose bodies could not be recovered. Any citizen or stranger who wishes joins the procession, and the female relatives are there to wail at the burial. The dead are laid in the public sepulchre in the most beautiful suburb of the city, where those who fall in war are always buried, with the exception of those killed at Marathon, who, for their singular and extraordinary valour, were interred on the spot where they fell. After the bodies have been laid in the earth, a man chosen by the state — of acknowledged wisdom and high reputation — delivers an appropriate eulogy over them; after which all retire. That is how the burial is conducted; and throughout the war, whenever the occasion arose, this established custom was followed. These were the first to have fallen, and Pericles, son of Xanthippus, was chosen to deliver their eulogy. When the right moment came, he advanced from the sepulchre to a raised platform so that he could be heard by as many of the crowd as possible, and spoke as follows:

“Most of those who have stood here before me have praised the man who added this speech to our funeral law, saying it is well that it should be delivered at the burial of those who fall in battle. For my own part, I would have thought that worth shown in deeds was sufficiently rewarded by honours also shown in deeds — such as you now see in this funeral provided at public cost. I would have wished that the reputations of many brave men were not put at risk in the mouth of a single individual, to stand or fall depending on whether he spoke well or badly. For it is hard to speak properly on a subject where it is hard even to convince your hearers that you are speaking the truth. On the one hand, the friend who knows every fact of the story may think some point has not been set out as fully as he wishes and as he knows it deserves; on the other, a stranger to the matter may be led by envy to suspect exaggeration if he hears anything beyond his own nature. For people can stand to hear others praised only as long as each can persuade himself that he is capable of equalling the deeds being recounted; once that point is passed, envy comes in, and with it disbelief. Still, since our ancestors have given this custom their approval, it is my duty to obey the law and to try to satisfy your several wishes and judgements as best I can.

“I will begin with our ancestors: it is just and proper that on an occasion like this they should have the honour of the first mention. They lived in this country from generation to generation in unbroken succession, and by their valour they handed it down free to the present day. If our more remote ancestors deserve praise, much more do our own fathers, who added to their inheritance the empire we now possess, and spared no pains to leave their gains to us of the present generation. And lastly, there are few parts of our dominions that have not been increased by us here, who are still more or less in the prime of life. The mother country has been furnished by us with everything she needs to depend on her own resources, whether for war or for peace. The military achievements that won us our various possessions, and the ready valour with which we or our fathers stemmed the tide of Hellenic or barbarian aggression — these are themes too familiar to my hearers for me to dwell on, and I will pass them by. But the path by which we reached our position, the form of government under which our greatness grew, the national habits out of which it sprang — these are questions I may try to answer before I move on to my eulogy of these men. I think the present occasion is one on which a speaker may properly dwell on these things, and on which the whole assembly, citizens and foreigners alike, may listen with profit.

“Our constitution does not copy the laws of neighbouring states; we are a model to others rather than imitators ourselves. Its administration favours the many instead of the few — that is why it is called a democracy. As for the laws, they afford equal justice to all in their private disputes; and where social standing is concerned, advancement in public life depends on a man’s reputation for ability, with class considerations not allowed to interfere with merit; nor does poverty bar the way — if a man is able to serve the state, he is not held back by the obscurity of his condition. The freedom we enjoy in our public life carries over into our private life. There, far from keeping a jealous watch on each other, we do not feel called on to be angry with our neighbour for doing as he likes, or even to give him those black looks that, though they carry no real penalty, cannot fail to give offence. But all this ease in our private dealings does not make us lawless as citizens. Our chief safeguard against this is fear, which teaches us to obey the magistrates and the laws, especially those that protect the injured — whether they are formally on the books or belong to that unwritten code which cannot be broken without acknowledged disgrace.

“Further, we provide plenty of opportunities for the mind to refresh itself from work. We hold games and sacrifices throughout the year, and the elegance of our private lives is a daily source of pleasure that helps to drive off gloom; while the size of our city draws the produce of the world into our harbour, so that for an Athenian the goods of other countries are as familiar a luxury as those of his own.

“If we turn to military matters, here too we differ from our adversaries. We throw our city open to the world, and never by alien acts shut foreigners out of any chance to learn or observe — even though the eyes of an enemy may sometimes profit from our openness. We trust less to system and policy than to the native spirit of our citizens. In education, where our rivals from their very cradles seek manliness through painful discipline, at Athens we live exactly as we please, and yet are just as ready to face every legitimate danger. Proof of this is that the Lacedaemonians do not invade our country alone but bring all their confederates with them, while we Athenians advance unsupported into a neighbour’s territory and, fighting on foreign soil, usually defeat with ease men who are defending their own homes. Our united force has never yet been met by any enemy, because we have to attend to our navy at the same time as we send our citizens by land on a hundred different services. So whenever the enemy engages with some fraction of our strength, a victory over a detachment is magnified into a victory over the whole nation, and a defeat into a setback at the hands of our entire people. And yet, if we are willing to face danger with habits of ease rather than of toil, with courage that is natural rather than the product of training, we have the double advantage of escaping the experience of hardships beforehand and of facing them, when the moment comes, as fearlessly as those who are never free of them.

“Nor are these the only points in which our city deserves admiration. We cultivate refinement without extravagance and knowledge without softness. We use wealth more for what it can do than for show, and we treat the real disgrace of poverty not as the admission of it but as the refusal to struggle against it. Our public men have, besides politics, their private affairs to attend to, and our ordinary citizens, though occupied with the pursuits of industry, are still fair judges of public matters. Unlike any other nation, we regard the man who takes no part in these duties not as unambitious but as useless. We Athenians are able to judge events even if we cannot originate them; and instead of treating discussion as a stumbling-block in the way of action, we think it an indispensable preliminary to wise action at all. Again, in our enterprises we present the singular spectacle of daring and deliberation, each carried to its highest point, and both united in the same persons; though usually decision is the fruit of ignorance and hesitation the fruit of reflection. But the palm for courage will surely be most justly given to those who best know the difference between hardship and pleasure and yet are never tempted to shrink from danger. In generosity too we are equally singular: we acquire our friends by conferring favours, not by receiving them. Of course, the doer of a favour is the firmer friend of the two, since by continued kindness he keeps the recipient in his debt; while the debtor feels less keenly, knowing that what he gives back will be a payment, not a free gift. And it is only the Athenians who, fearless of consequences, confer their benefits not from calculations of expediency but in the confidence of liberality.

“In short, I say that as a city we are the school of Hellas; and I doubt the world can produce a man who, when he has only himself to depend on, is equal to so many emergencies and graced with such happy versatility as the Athenian. That this is no mere boast thrown out for the occasion, but plain matter of fact, the power our state has won by these habits proves. For Athens alone among her contemporaries is found, when tested, to be greater than her reputation. She alone gives no occasion to her assailants to blush at the antagonist by whom they have been beaten, nor to her subjects to question her right to rule by merit. The admiration of this age and the next will be ours, since we have not left our power without witness but have shown it by mighty proofs. Far from needing a Homer to praise us, or any other of his craft whose verses might charm for the moment but whose impression would melt at the touch of fact, we have forced every sea and every land to be the highway of our daring, and everywhere, for evil or for good, have left imperishable monuments behind us. Such is the Athens for which these men, in the assertion of their resolve not to lose her, nobly fought and died; and well may every one of their survivors be ready to suffer in her cause.

“If I have dwelt at some length on the character of our country, it is to show that our stake in this struggle is not the same as that of men who have no such blessings to lose, and also that the eulogy of the men I am now speaking over may be established by definite proofs. That eulogy is now in great part complete; for the Athens I have praised is only what the heroism of these men and their like have made her — men whose fame, unlike that of most Hellenes, will be found to match their deserts exactly. And if a test of worth is wanted, it is to be found in their final scene, and not only in cases where it set the final seal on their merit, but also in cases where it gave the first sign of their having any. For there is justice in the claim that steadfastness in his country’s battles should serve as a cloak to cover a man’s other faults; the good action has wiped out the bad, and his merit as a citizen has more than outweighed his shortcomings as an individual. None of these men allowed wealth, with its prospect of future enjoyment, to unnerve his spirit, or poverty, with its hope of one day being free and rich, to tempt him to shrink from danger. They held that vengeance on their enemies was more to be desired than any personal blessings, and judging this to be the most glorious of risks, they joyfully chose to take it — to make sure of their vengeance and to let their wishes wait. Committing to hope the uncertainty of final success, in the business before them they thought it right to act boldly and trust in themselves. Choosing to die resisting rather than to live submitting, they fled only from dishonour but met danger face to face; and after one brief moment, while at the height of their fortune, they passed away — not from their fear, but from their glory.

“So these men died as Athenians should. You, their survivors, must resolve to be no less unwavering on the field, though you may pray that your resolve may have a happier outcome. Do not be content with ideas of the advantages bound up with the defence of your country drawn from words alone, however valuable a text these might furnish to a speaker even before an audience as alive to them as this one. You must yourselves grasp the power of Athens and feed your eyes upon her day after day, until love of her fills your hearts. Then, when all her greatness breaks upon you, reflect that it was by courage, by a sense of duty, and by a keen feeling of honour in action that men were able to win all this; and that no personal failure in an enterprise could make them consent to deprive their country of their valour, but they laid it at her feet as the most glorious offering they could give. For this offering of their lives, made in common by them all, each of them individually received that renown which never grows old; and for a sepulchre, not so much that in which their bones lie, but the noblest of shrines, where their glory is laid up to be eternally remembered on every occasion when deed or story shall call for its commemoration. For heroes have the whole earth as their tomb; and in lands far from their own, where the column with its epitaph proclaims it, there is enshrined in every breast a record unwritten, with no tablet to preserve it but that of the heart. Take these men as your model, and judging happiness to be the fruit of freedom and freedom of valour, never decline the dangers of war. It is not the wretched who are most justified in being unsparing of their lives — they have nothing to hope for. It is rather those for whom continued life may bring reverses still unknown, and to whom a fall, if it came, would be most catastrophic in its consequences. Surely, to a man of spirit, the degradation of cowardice must be far more grievous than an unfelt death that strikes him at the height of his strength and patriotism.

“Comfort, therefore — not condolence — is what I have to offer the parents of the dead who may be here. The chances to which the life of man is subject are countless, as they know; but fortunate indeed are those who draw for their lot a death so glorious as the one that has caused your mourning, and to whom life has been so exactly measured that it ends in the happiness in which it was passed. Still, I know this is a hard saying, especially when those you have lost will be brought constantly to mind by seeing in the homes of others blessings of which you too once boasted; for grief is felt not so much for the lack of what we have never known as for the loss of what we have long been used to. Yet you who are still of an age to have children must bear up in the hope of having others in their place; not only will they help you to forget those you have lost, but they will be a reinforcement and a security to the state, since no fair or just policy can be expected of the citizen who does not, like his fellows, bring to the decision the interests and apprehensions of a father. Those of you who are past your prime must take comfort in the thought that the best part of your life was fortunate, and that the brief span that remains will be cheered by the fame of the departed. For only the love of honour never grows old; and it is honour, not gain, as some would have it, that gladdens the heart of age and helplessness.

“Turning to the sons or brothers of the dead, I see that an arduous struggle lies before you. When a man is gone, all are accustomed to praise him; and however transcendent your merit, you will still find it hard not only to overtake but even to come close to their renown. The living have envy to contend with, while those who are no longer in our path are honoured with a goodwill into which rivalry does not enter. On the other hand, if I must say anything to those of you who will now be in widowhood, I will sum it up in this brief charge. Great will be your glory in not falling short of your natural character; and greatest will be hers who is least talked of among men, whether for good or for ill.

“My task is now finished. I have done it as well as I could; and in word, at least, the requirements of the law are now satisfied. As for deeds, those buried here have already received part of their honours, and for the rest, their children shall be brought up to manhood at public expense. The state thus offers a valuable prize, as a garland of victory in this race of valour, both for the fallen and for their survivors. And where the rewards for merit are greatest, there the best citizens are found.
“And now that you have made an end of your lamentations for your relatives, you may depart.”
